method: An edge-grain board is a row of strips glued face to face: the rip strip width w sets how much of the board width each strip contributes, so the strip count is ceil(finished width / w), the glued board is strips x w wide, and the stock thickness after flattening becomes the board thickness. The lumber consumed across the width is the summed strip widths plus one kerf between every neighbouring pair, strips x w + (strips - 1) x kerf, and the lumber length is the finished length plus the trim allowance at each end. An end-grain board turns that panel on edge: the strips are ripped so their width runs across the finished board length, making the board length strips x w; the panel is then crosscut into slices as thick as the finished board, each slice is rotated a quarter turn and glued face to face, so the slice count is ceil(finished width / finished thickness), the board width is slices x thickness, and the panel length is that width plus one kerf between slices plus the trim at both ends. The end-grain board thickness is the flattened panel thickness, which is why the stock must be at least as thick as the finished board in both builds. Board feet are the purchased lumber volume, stock width x stock length x stock thickness, converted at 1 board foot = 2,359,737.216 mm3 (144 in3). Lengths are entered in millimetres or inches and converted at 25.4 mm per inch. Kerf must be narrower than the strip, strips and slices are capped at 60, and the page warns when a strip is under 20 mm, when the blade removes more than 40% of a rip, when under 2 mm is left for flattening, and when rounding up leaves more than half a strip or slice over the asked size. Glue-line thickness, planing after the first glue-up, snipe, re-squaring the panel and the offcut from rounding up are not modelled, so the figures are a shopping allowance rather than a cut list.
